claim: GPCRs play critical roles in cell communication.
source: GPCRs play critical roles in cell communication.
evidence: This is a general statement about GPCRs that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: GPCRs can form heteromers.
source: Although GPCRs can form heteromers, their role in signaling remains elusive.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to scientific literature on GPCR heteromers.

claim: The role of GPCR heteromers in signaling remains elusive.
source: Although GPCRs can form heteromers, their role in signaling remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: mGluRs can form both constitutive homo- and heterodimers.
source: mGluRs can form both constitutive homo- and heterodimers.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on mGluR dimerization.

claim: Both mGlu2 and mGlu4 couple to G proteins.
source: Whereas both mGlu2 and mGlu4 couple to G proteins, G protein activation is mediated by mGlu4 heptahelical domain (HD) exclusively in mGlu2-4 heterodimers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: G protein activation is mediated by mGlu4 heptahelical domain (HD) exclusively in mGlu2-4 heterodimers.
source: Whereas both mGlu2 and mGlu4 couple to G proteins, G protein activation is mediated by mGlu4 heptahelical domain (HD) exclusively in mGlu2-4 heterodimers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Asymmetric transduction in mGlu2-4 heterodimers results from the action of both the dimeric extracellular domain and an allosteric activation by the partially-activated non-functional mGlu2 HD.
source: Such asymmetric transduction results from the action of both the dimeric extracellular domain, and an allosteric activation by the partially-activated non-functional mGlu2 HD.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: G proteins activation by mGlu2 HD occurs if the mGlu2 HD is occupied by a positive allosteric modulator.
source: G proteins activation by mGlu2 HD occurs if either the mGlu2 HD is occupied by a positive allosteric modulator or if mGlu4 HD is inhibited by a negative modulator.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with allosteric modulators.

claim: G proteins activation by mGlu2 HD occurs if mGlu4 HD is inhibited by a negative modulator.
source: G proteins activation by mGlu2 HD occurs if either the mGlu2 HD is occupied by a positive allosteric modulator or if mGlu4 HD is inhibited by a negative modulator.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with allosteric modulators.

claim: There is an oriented asymmetry in mGlu heterodimers that can be controlled with allosteric modulators.
source: These data revealed an oriented asymmetry in mGlu heterodimers that can be controlled with allosteric modulators.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claim: Many cell surface receptors form multi-protein complexes for signaling integration.
source: Many cell surface receptors form multi-protein complexes for signaling integration (Klingenberg, 1981; Salter, 2003; Altier et al., 2006; González-Maeso et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GPCRs are the most abundant cell surface receptors.
source: Among them, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the most abundant and constitute the main targets in drug development (Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: GPCRs constitute the main targets in drug development.
source: Among them, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the most abundant and constitute the main targets in drug development (Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Most GPCRs can signal in a monomeric form.
source: Although most GPCRs can signal in a monomeric form (El Moustaine et al., 2012; White et al., 2007; Whorton et al., 2007), increasing studies revealed that they can associate into both homo and heteromeric complexes (Prezeau et al., 2010; Ferré et al., 2014; Gomes et al., 2016; Maurel et al., 2008; Albizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GPCRs can associate into both homo and heteromeric complexes.
source: Although most GPCRs can signal in a monomeric form (El Moustaine et al., 2012; White et al., 2007; Whorton et al., 2007), increasing studies revealed that they can associate into both homo and heteromeric complexes (Prezeau et al., 2010; Ferré et al., 2014; Gomes et al., 2016; Maurel et al., 2008; Albizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: GPCR heteromers may generate original functional pharmacological entities different from each of the homomers.
source: Interestingly, GPCR heteromers may generate original functional pharmacological entities different from each of the homomers (Ferré et al., 2014; Gomes et al., 2016; Bellot et al., 2015; Wertman and Dupré, 2013; Fribourg et al., 2011; Urizar et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Whether GPCR association is real in native tissue is still a matter of intense debate.
source: Whether such GPCR association is real in native tissue is still a matter of intense debate (Bouvier and Hébert, 2014; Lambert and Javitch, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents the current state of the field.

claim: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C GPCRs.
source: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C GPCRs and are well-recognized constitutive homodimers (Kniazeff et al., 2011; Pin and Bettler, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mGluRs are well-recognized constitutive homodimers.
source: Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) are class C GPCRs and are well-recognized constitutive homodimers (Kniazeff et al., 2011; Pin and Bettler, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mGluRs are divided into three groups: group I (mGlu1,5), II (mGlu2,3) and III (mGlu4,6,7,8), on the basis of sequence homology, pharmacological profile and cellular signaling.
source: These receptors are divided into three groups: group I (mGlu1,5), II (mGlu2,3) and III (mGlu4,6,7,8), on the basis of sequence homology, pharmacological profile and cellular signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mGluR classification.

claim: mGluRs were shown to also form heterodimers with specific subunit composition.
source: Recently, mGluRs were shown to also form heterodimers with specific subunit composition (Doumazane et al., 2011; Kammermeier, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of mGlu1 and 5.
source: Of note, whereas the different mGluRs were commonly described as having specific brain distribution supporting their homodimeric nature, localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of different mGluRs such as mGlu1 and 5 (Pandya et al., 2016), mGlu2 and 4 (Yin et al., 2014), mGlu7 and 8 (Ferraguti et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of mGlu2 and 4.
source: Of note, whereas the different mGluRs were commonly described as having specific brain distribution supporting their homodimeric nature, localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of different mGluRs such as mGlu1 and 5 (Pandya et al., 2016), mGlu2 and 4 (Yin et al., 2014), mGlu7 and 8 (Ferraguti et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of mGlu7 and 8.
source: Of note, whereas the different mGluRs were commonly described as having specific brain distribution supporting their homodimeric nature, localization studies revealed subcellular co-localization of different mGluRs such as mGlu1 and 5 (Pandya et al., 2016), mGlu2 and 4 (Yin et al., 2014), mGlu7 and 8 (Ferraguti et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies supported the existence of mGlu2-4 and 1–5 heterodimers in the brain.
source: Further studies supported the existence of mGlu2-4 and 1–5 heterodimers in the brain (Pandya et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2014; Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Homodimeric mGlu4, rather than heterodimeric mGlu2-4, were proposed as a better target for Parkinson's disease treatment.
source: Being identified very recently, not much is known about the possible clinical relevance of mGlu heterodimers, but already homodimeric mGlu4, rather than heterodimeric mGlu2-4, were proposed as a better target for Parkinson's disease treatment (Niswender et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mGlu2-4 heterodimers control synaptic activity at the level of the cortico-striatal terminals in the striatum.
source: In contrast, mGlu2-4 heterodimers control synaptic activity at the level of the cortico-striatal terminals in the striatum (Yin et al., 2014) and lateral perforant path terminals in the dendate gyrus (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mGlu2-4 heterodimers control synaptic activity at the level of lateral perforant path terminals in the dendate gyrus.
source: In contrast, mGlu2-4 heterodimers control synaptic activity at the level of the cortico-striatal terminals in the striatum (Yin et al., 2014) and lateral perforant path terminals in the dendate gyrus (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mGlu subunits are multidomain proteins composed of a Venus flytrap domain (VFT) containing the orthosteric binding site, connected via a cysteine-rich domain (CRD) to a heptahelical domain (HD) involved in G protein coupling.
source: The mGlu subunits are multidomain proteins composed of a Venus flytrap domain (VFT) containing the orthosteric binding site, connected via a cysteine-rich domain (CRD) to a heptahelical domain (HD) involved in G protein coupling (Pin and Bettler, 2016; Wu et al., 2014; Doré et al., 2014; Kunishima et al., 2000; Tsuchiya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Structural and biophysical studies revealed a symmetrical conformational change during activation at the level of the VFTs in mGlu homodimers.
source: In the case of mGlu homodimers, structural and biophysical studies revealed a symmetrical conformational change during activation at the level of the VFTs (Doumazane et al., 2013; Rondard et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2011; Xue et al., 2015; Olofsson et al., 2014; Vafabakhsh et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Activating one VFT is sufficient to partially activate the homodimers.
source: Indeed, while activating one VFT is sufficient to partially activate the homodimers, activating both VFTs is required for full activity both in homodimeric (Kniazeff et al., 2004; Brock et al., 2007; Levitz et al., 2016) and heterodimeric receptors (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activating both VFTs is required for full activity in homodimeric receptors.
source: Indeed, while activating one VFT is sufficient to partially activate the homodimers, activating both VFTs is required for full activity both in homodimeric (Kniazeff et al., 2004; Brock et al., 2007; Levitz et al., 2016) and heterodimeric receptors (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activating both VFTs is required for full activity in heterodimeric receptors.
source: Indeed, while activating one VFT is sufficient to partially activate the homodimers, activating both VFTs is required for full activity both in homodimeric (Kniazeff et al., 2004; Brock et al., 2007; Levitz et al., 2016) and heterodimeric receptors (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Symmetric activation of the VFT dimer leads to an asymmetric activation of the HD dimer, only one HD being active at a time.
source: Surprisingly, this symmetric activation of the VFT dimer leads to an asymmetric activation of the HD dimer, only one HD being active at a time (Hlavackova et al., 2012; Hlavackova et al., 2005; Goudet et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The existence of mGlu2-4 heterodimer in the brain has been documented.
source: In this study, we choose mGlu2-4 heterodimer as a prototype heterodimer, as its existence in the brain has been documented (Yin et al., 2014; Moreno Delgado et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Only mGlu4 HD activates G proteins in mGlu2-4 heterodimers.
source: We show that whereas both mGlu2 and mGlu4 HDs are capable of activating G proteins, only mGlu4 HD does it in mGlu2-4 heterodimers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A conformational change in the mGlu2 HD occurs that can be prevented by a mGlu2 negative allosteric modulator (NAM).
source: Although a conformational change in the mGlu2 HD occurs that can be prevented by a mGlu2 negative allosteric modulator (NAM), it is not sufficient for a direct activation of G proteins, but important for the G protein coupling by the associated mGlu4 HD.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The conformational change in mGlu2 HD is not sufficient for a direct activation of G proteins, but important for the G protein coupling by the associated mGlu4 HD.
source: Although a conformational change in the mGlu2 HD occurs that can be prevented by a mGlu2 negative allosteric modulator (NAM), it is not sufficient for a direct activation of G proteins, but important for the G protein coupling by the associated mGlu4 HD.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Manipulating the conformation of either mGlu2 or mGlu4 HD with positive and negative allosteric modulators can reorient the asymmetry towards mGlu2 activating G proteins.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that manipulating the conformation of either mGlu2 or mGlu4 HD with positive and negative allosteric modulators can reorient the asymmetry towards mGlu2 activating G proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: There is a differential ability of mGlu2 and mGlu4 HD to reach a G protein activating state.
source: This demonstrates a differential ability of mGlu2 and mGlu4 HD to reach a G protein activating state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There are strong allosteric interactions between two GPCRs in a dimeric complex.
source: But most importantly, these data reveal strong allosteric interactions between two GPCRs in a dimeric complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Allosteric coupling between GPCRs in a dimeric complex can be controlled with small molecules allosteric modulators.
source: Such allosteric coupling can be controlled with small molecules allosteric modulators revealing a way to modulate heteromeric receptor activity, and expanding the possibilities of using such small molecules to precisely control signaling events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Chimeric mGlu2 and mGlu4 subunits containing complementary coiled-coil regions (C1 and C2) derived from the GABAB receptor and intracellular retention signals (KKXX) were engineered.
source: We then used a quality control system that allows cell surface targeting of the heterodimer only (Brock et al., 2007). We engineered chimeric mGlu2 and mGlu4 subunits containing complementary coiled-coil regions (C1 and C2) derived from the GABAB receptor and intracellular retention signals (KKXX) (Huang et al., 2011; Kniazeff et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: By combination of C1 and C2 containing subunits, mGlu2-4 heterodimers can be obtained specifically at the cell surface, as well as the mGlu2 (2-2) and mGlu4 (4-4) homodimers as controls.
source: By combination of C1 and C2 containing subunits, we can obtain the mGlu2-4 heterodimers specifically at the cell surface, as well as the mGlu2 (2-2) and mGlu4 (4-4) homodimers as controls (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by Figure 1A,B.

claim: Receptor constructs with C1 and C2 retained their ability to activate G proteins when at the cell surface.
source: Such receptor constructs retained their ability to activate G proteins (we used the chimeric Gqi and Gqo proteins that enable coupling of these receptors to the PLC pathway [Conklin et al., 1993; Blahos et al., 1998]) when at the cell surface, with the expected action of mGlu2 (DCG-IV) and mGlu4 (L-AP4) selective agonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When activated with glutamate, mGlu2 and mGlu2-4 displayed a similar potency and efficacy.
source: When activated with glutamate, mGlu2 and mGlu2-4 displayed a similar potency and efficacy, while glutamate had a lower efficacy at mGlu4 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Glutamate had a lower efficacy at mGlu4.
source: When activated with glutamate, mGlu2 and mGlu2-4 displayed a similar potency and efficacy, while glutamate had a lower efficacy at mGlu4 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All receptor combinations were expressed at a similar level at the cell surface.
source: Note that all these receptor combinations were expressed at a similar level at the cell surface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutating the conserved Phe residue into Ser in the third intracellular loop of mGluRs abolished their ability to activate G proteins.
source: Mutating the conserved Phe residue into Ser in the third intracellular loop of mGluRs abolished their ability to activate G proteins (Kniazeff et al., 2004; Hlavackova et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither mGlu2-F756S, nor mGlu4-F781S activated G proteins.
source: When introduced into the C1 and C2 constructs, neither mGlu2-F756S, nor mGlu4-F781S activated G proteins (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: When only one subunit carries the FS mutation, a larger decrease in glutamate efficacy was observed in mGlu2 dimers than in mGlu4 dimers.
source: When only one subunit carries the mutation, a larger decrease in glutamate efficacy was observed in mGlu2 dimers than in mGlu4 dimers (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: When the FS mutation was introduced in the mGlu2 subunit of the mGlu2-4 heterodimer, a glutamate-mediated response similar to the control was observed.
source: When such mutation was introduced in the mGlu2 subunit of the mGlu2-4 heterodimer, a glutamate-mediated response similar to the control was observed (Figure 1D,F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: In the heterodimer containing the mutated mGlu4 subunit no response could be observed.
source: In contrast, in the heterodimer containing the mutated mGlu4 subunit no response could be observed (Figure 1F) despite a correct expression level at the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introducing the FS mutation in both subunits of mGlu2-4 heterodimer abolished glutamate-induced G protein signaling.
source: As a control, introducing the FS mutation in both subunits of mGlu2-4 heterodimer abolished glutamate-induced G protein signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Signal could be generated with the heterodimers mutated in the mGlu2 subunit when the selective mGlu2 and mGlu4 agonists DCG-IV and L-AP4 were used.
source: Even when the selective mGlu2 and mGlu4 agonists DCG-IV and L-AP4 were used, signal could be generated with the heterodimers mutated in the mGlu2 subunit, but not in those mutated in the mGlu4 subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: Signal could not be generated with the heterodimers mutated in the mGlu4 subunits when the selective mGlu2 and mGlu4 agonists DCG-IV and L-AP4 were used.
source: Even when the selective mGlu2 and mGlu4 agonists DCG-IV and L-AP4 were used, signal could be generated with the heterodimers mutated in the mGlu2 subunit, but not in those mutated in the mGlu4 subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: In the heterodimer, G protein activation is exclusively mediated by mGlu4 HD.
source: Such data strongly suggest that in the heterodimer, G protein activation is exclusively mediated by mGlu4 HD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Similar results were obtained with either mGlu2C1-4C2 or 4C1-2C2 heterodimers, indicating that the modified C terminal domains do not influence the asymmetric activation.
source: Of note, similar results were obtained with either mGlu2C1-4C2 or 4C1-2C2 heterodimers, indicating that the modified C terminal domains do not influence the asymmetric activation (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,F.

claim: For any of the receptor combinations containing two mGlu2 VFTs, two mGlu4 VFTs, or in which the VFTs were swapped between the two subunits, a correct and specific expression of any of the indicated dimer combinations at the cell surface could be verified.
source: Thanks to the C1 C2 terminal tails, a correct and specific expression of any of the indicated dimer combinations at the cell surface could be verified thanks to the HA or Flag N-terminal epitopes (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: When activated by glutamate, any combination carrying a wild-type mGlu4 HD (with or without a mutated mGlu2 HD) generated Ca2+ signals.
source: When activated by glutamate, we found that any combination carrying a wild-type mGlu4 HD (with or without a mutated mGlu2 HD) generated Ca2+ signals (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the receptor combinations carrying a mutated mGlu4 HD were functional.
source: In contrast, none of those carrying a mutated mGlu4 HD were functional (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) despite their expression at the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activating specifically the mGlu2 VFT with DCG-IV, or the mGlu4 VFT with L-AP4 led to G protein signaling of receptor combinations carrying at least one mGlu2 VFT, or one mGlu4 VFT, respectively, as long as the receptor contained a wild-type mGlu4 HD.
source: Similarly, activating specifically the mGlu2 VFT with DCG-IV, or the mGlu4 VFT with L-AP4 led to G protein signaling of receptor combinations carrying at least one mGlu2 VFT, or one mGlu4 VFT, respectively, as long as the receptor contained a wild-type mGlu4 HD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: No response could be generated with these agonists in receptor combinations carrying a mutated mGlu4 HD.
source: No response could be generated with these agonists in receptor combinations carrying a mutated mGlu4 HD (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating position 521 of the mGlu2 CRD to Cys led to a fully active dimer (mGlu2C).
source: We previously reported that an inter-subunit disulfide bound between a Cys introduced at position 521 of the mGlu2 CRD led to a fully active dimer (mGlu2C) (Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutating the equivalent position in mGlu4 (His523Cys) also generated a fully active receptor (mGlu4C).
source: Mutating the equivalent position in mGlu4 (His523Cys) also generated a fully active receptor (mGlu4C) (Figure 3A), as revealed by the accumulation of inositol monophosphate after LiCl addition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When both mGlu2C and mGlu4C were co-expressed, an inter-subunit DTT-sensitive covalent linkage could be demonstrated.
source: When both mGlu2C and mGlu4C were co-expressed, an inter-subunit DTT-sensitive covalent linkage could be demonstrated, providing the natural inter-VFT disulfide bound is mutated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The receptor combination with both mGlu2C and mGlu4C displayed a full constitutive activity.
source: Such a receptor combination also displayed a full constitutive activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The high constitutive or glutamate-induced signaling could be observed in the heterodimer combinations containing a wild-type mGlu4 HD but not in those in which the mGlu4 HD contained the FS mutation.
source: In that case again, the high constitutive or glutamate-induced signaling could be observed in the heterodimer combinations containing a wild-type mGlu4 HD but not in those in which the mGlu4 HD contained the FS mutation (Figure 3A) despite a correct expression of all constructs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Any ways the dimeric ECD of the mGlu2-4 heterodimer is activated the mGlu4 HD is always responsible for G protein activation.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that any ways the dimeric ECD of the mGlu2-4 heterodimer is activated the mGlu4 HD is always responsible for G protein activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The asymmetric activity of the mGlu2-4 HD dimer is an intrinsic property of this membrane part of the receptor.
source: This strongly suggests that the asymmetric activity of the mGlu2-4 HD dimer is an intrinsic property of this membrane part of the receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MNI137 is an mGlu2 NAM known to stabilize the mGlu2 HD in its inactive conformation.
source: We then used MNI137, an mGlu2 NAM (Hemstapat et al., 2007) known to stabilize the mGlu2 HD in its inactive conformation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: MNI137 partially inhibited mGlu2-4 heterodimer.
source: We found that MNI137 partially inhibited mGlu2-4 heterodimer while it largely inhibited the response of the mGlu2 homodimer, whether the dimer was activated by glutamate (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1) or was constitutively active through the inter-CRD disulfide bridge (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: MNI137 largely inhibited the response of the mGlu2 homodimer.
source: We found that MNI137 partially inhibited mGlu2-4 heterodimer while it largely inhibited the response of the mGlu2 homodimer, whether the dimer was activated by glutamate (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1) or was constitutively active through the inter-CRD disulfide bridge (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Similar data were obtained in a receptor combination in which the mGlu2 subunit is incapable of G protein coupling.
source: Of note, similar data were obtained in a receptor combination in which the mGlu2 subunit is incapable of G protein coupling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A conformational change in the mGlu2 HD prevented by MNI137 binding is required to fully activate the mGlu4 HD.
source: This revealed that a conformational change in the mGlu2 HD prevented by MNI137 binding is required to fully activate the mGlu4 HD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MNI137 blocked mGlu2-4 heterodimer signaling induced by either DCG-IV or L-AP4 respectively.
source: Interestingly, we found that MNI137 blocked mGlu2-4 heterodimer signaling induced by either DCG-IV or L-AP4 respectively whereas MNI137 inhibited only partially signaling induced by the combination of DCG IV and L-AP4 as observed with glutamate (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: MNI137 inhibited only partially signaling induced by the combination of DCG IV and L-AP4 as observed with glutamate.
source: Interestingly, we found that MNI137 blocked mGlu2-4 heterodimer signaling induced by either DCG-IV or L-AP4 respectively whereas MNI137 inhibited only partially signaling induced by the combination of DCG IV and L-AP4 as observed with glutamate (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: mGlu2 HD plays a prominent role in activating mGlu4 HD when only one VFT is activated.
source: These data revealed the prominent role of mGlu2 HD in activating mGlu4 HD when only one VFT is activated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activation of both VFTs with DCG-IV in receptor combinations containing two mGlu2 VFTs is only partially inhibited by MNI137, with a smaller inhibition (39.2 ± 4.7%, n = 3) when both CRDs are from mGlu2, compared to the situation where the mGlu4 HD is associated with the mGlu4 CRD (64.3 ± 3.8% inhibition, n = 3, p<0.05).
source: Consistent with this conclusion, activation of both VFTs with DCG-IV in receptor combinations containing two mGlu2 VFTs is only partially inhibited by MNI137, with a smaller inhibition (39.2 ± 4.7%, n = 3) when both CRDs are from mGlu2, compared to the situation where the mGlu4 HD is associated with the mGlu4 CRD (64.3 ± 3.8% inhibition, n = 3, p<0.05) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: OptoGluNAM4.1 is an mGlu4 NAM that prevents mGlu4 HD activation.
source: We first analyzed the effect of an mGlu4 NAM (OptoGluNAM4.1) that we recently reported to prevent mGlu4 HD activation (Rovira et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: OptoGluNAM4.1, while inhibiting agonist-mediated mGlu4 activity, had no effect on the mGlu2-4 heterodimer.
source: Surprisingly, this compound, while inhibiting agonist-mediated mGlu4 activity (Rovira et al., 2016), had no effect on the mGlu2-4 heterodimer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When using an mGlu2-4 combination in which the mGlu4 HD is unable to activate G protein, the addition of OptoGluNAM4.1 allowed glutamate to generate a signal.
source: Most interestingly, when using an mGlu2-4 combination in which the mGlu4 HD is unable to activate G protein, then a heterodimer unable to activate G proteins, the addition of OptoGluNAM4.1 allowed glutamate to generate a signal (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: By preventing mGlu4 HD to reach its active state, mGlu2 HD can take over for G protein activation in the heterodimer.
source: This suggests that, by preventing mGlu4 HD to reach its active state, mGlu2 HD can take over for G protein activation in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The mGlu2 PAM LY487379 had no significant effect on the mGlu2-4 heterodimer signaling capacity.
source: This compound had no significant effect on the mGlu2-4 heterodimer signaling capacity (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1) or on the mGlu2-4 heterodimer mutated in mGlu2 HD (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: On the non-functional mGlu2-4 combination where the mGlu4 HD is mutated, the mGlu2 PAM LY487379 allowed glutamate to activate G proteins.
source: However, on the non-functional mGlu2-4 combination where the mGlu4 HD is mutated, the mGlu2 PAM LY487379 allowed glutamate to activate G proteins, therefore revealing a possible coupling of the mGlu2 HD in this heterodimer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Under normal conditions, the coupling of mGlu2-4 is mediated by mGlu4 HD, but the mGlu2 HD can still generate signaling providing its activation is facilitated by a PAM, or by the inhibition of mGlu4 HD with a NAM.
source: Taken together, these data revealed that under normal conditions, the coupling of mGlu2-4 is mediated by mGlu4 HD, but the mGlu2 HD can still generate signaling providing its activation is facilitated by a PAM, or by the inhibition of mGlu4 HD with a NAM (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The asymmetric activation of the mGlu2-4 HDs is not the consequence of the presence of the C1-C2 intracellular domains.
source: These data confirmed that the asymmetric activation of the mGlu2-4 HDs is not the consequence of the presence of the C1-C2 intracellular domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In all heterodimers made of mGlu2 or mGlu3 associated with any of the group-III mGluRs (mGlu4, 6, 7 and 8), the group-III subunit is responsible for G protein activation.
source: As depicted in Figure 6C–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, similar data were obtained with any of these 4 types of heterodimers for mGlu2 and for mGlu3. These data indicate that in all these cases, the group-III subunit is responsible for G protein activation in these heterodimers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mGlu2 NAM, MNI137, inhibited signaling of all heterodimers made of mGlu2 or mGlu3 associated with any of the group-III mGluRs.
source: As observed with the mGlu2-4 heterodimer (Figure 4), the mGlu2 NAM, MNI137, inhibited signaling of all these heterodimers (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C–F.

claim: The mGlu2 HD, though not directly involved in G protein coupling, is important to allow the group-III subunit to signal in these heterodimeric receptors.
source: This is consistent with the mGlu2 HD, though not directly involved in G protein coupling, being important to allow the group-III subunit to signal in these heterodimeric receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In the mGlu2-4 heterodimer, only the mGlu4 subunit activates G proteins.
source: Our data revealed important information on how two G protein-activating units communicate within a heterodimeric complex. We found that in the mGlu2-4 heterodimer, only the mGlu4 subunit activates G proteins, and we revealed a complex allosteric interaction between the two HDs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: There is a complex allosteric interaction between the two HDs in the mGlu2-4 heterodimer.
source: Our data revealed important information on how two G protein-activating units communicate within a heterodimeric complex. We found that in the mGlu2-4 heterodimer, only the mGlu4 subunit activates G proteins, and we revealed a complex allosteric interaction between the two HDs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The mGlu2 subunit retains its ability to signal providing its activation is favored using mGlu2 PAMs, or preventing the activation of mGlu4 HD with a NAM.
source: Indeed, the mGlu2 subunit retains its ability to signal providing its activation is favored using mGlu2 PAMs, or preventing the activation of mGlu4 HD with a NAM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Even in the mGlu homodimers, only one subunit is active at a time, although in that case, each subunit has the same probability of being active.
source: Such asymmetric activation of a GPCR dimer has often been observed (Vilardaga et al., 2008; Han et al., 2009; Galvez et al., 2001; Duthey et al., 2002; Levoye et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2004). Even in the mGlu homodimers, only one subunit is active at a time, although in that case, each subunit has the same probability of being active (Hlavackova et al., 2012; Hlavackova et al., 2005; Goudet et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For the heterodimeric GABAB and T1R taste receptors, one subunit only is responsible for G protein activation.
source: For the well-characterized heterodimeric GPCRs, such as the GABAB and the T1R taste receptors, also one subunit only is responsible for G protein activation (Galvez et al., 2001; Duthey et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2004), although this was assumed to result from the inability of the other subunit to signal.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The inability of signaling of one subunit may result from an inhibitory effect of the other subunit while in its fully active state.
source: Our data suggest that instead, the inability of signaling of one subunit may result from an inhibitory effect of the other subunit while in its fully active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The GABAB1 subunit, not involved in coupling in the heterodimer, has been reported to signal when expressed alone.
source: This is indeed likely the case for the GABAB receptor for which the GABAB1 subunit, not involved in coupling in the heterodimer, has been reported to signal when expressed alone (Baloucoune et al., 2012; Richer et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Similar asymmetric coupling has been reported for class A GPCR heterodimers, where the activation of one receptor prevents the activation of the other.
source: Similar asymmetric coupling has also been reported for class A GPCR heterodimers, where the activation of one receptor prevents the activation of the other (Vilardaga et al., 2008; Han et al., 2009; Levoye et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a strong negative cooperativity between the HDs in a dimeric GPCR complex, where the activation of one subunit suppresses the ability of the other to signal.
source: These observations reinforce the idea of a strong negative cooperativity between the HDs in a dimeric GPCR complex, where the activation of one subunit suppresses the ability of the other to signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous research.

claim: Numerous studies report negative cooperativity in agonist binding on dimeric GPCRs.
source: This conclusion is further supported by numerous studies reporting negative cooperativity in agonist binding on dimeric GPCRs (Albizu et al., 2010; Urizar et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The coupling efficacy of mGlu4 homodimer is lower than that of mGlu2.
source: While mGlu4 homodimer coupling efficacy measured is lower than that of mGlu2, it is interesting to note that the coupling efficacy of mGlu2-4 heterodimer is similar to that of mGlu2 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The coupling efficacy of mGlu2-4 heterodimer is similar to that of mGlu2 receptors.
source: While mGlu4 homodimer coupling efficacy measured is lower than that of mGlu2, it is interesting to note that the coupling efficacy of mGlu2-4 heterodimer is similar to that of mGlu2 receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The mGlu2 subunit potentiates mGlu4 efficacy.
source: Because in both mGlu4 and mGlu2-4, the G protein activation is mediated by the mGlu4 HD, this means that the mGlu2 subunit potentiates mGlu4 efficacy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The low coupling efficacy of mGlu4 homodimers may be the consequence of a weaker action of the mGlu4 ECD dimer on the HDs.
source: Such a low coupling efficacy of mGlu4 homodimers may well be the consequence of a weaker action of the mGlu4 ECD dimer on the HDs, consistent with the weaker coupling of heterodimers containing two mGlu4 ECDs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The mGlu2 HD likely changes its conformation to exert a positive effect on mGlu4 HD activation, even though this conformation is not sufficient for G protein coupling.
source: Indeed, the mGlu2 HD likely changes its conformation to exert this positive effect, even though this conformation is not sufficient for G protein coupling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The action of the mGlu2 HD is even more prominent if the VFT dimer is asymmetrically activated, with only one VFT occupied by an agonist.
source: Such an action of the mGlu2 HD is even more prominent if the VFT dimer is asymmetrically activated, with only one VFT occupied by an agonist (Figure 7, States 3b, 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The GABAB1 HD is involved in a direct activation of the GABAB2 HD through an intra-molecular conformational change.
source: They are however perfectly in line with the role of the GABAB1 HD in the activation process of the heterodimeric GABAB receptor, the latter being involved in a direct activation of the GABAB2 HD through an intra-molecular conformational change (Monnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The activation of one HD within the dimer is controlled by the reorientation of the VFTs with an efficient coupling when the reorientation is symmetric (both VFTs activated), and a less efficient coupling in case only one VFT is activated.
source: The first one is by the reorientation of the VFTs with an efficient coupling when the reorientation is symmetric (both VFTs activated), and a less efficient coupling in case only one VFT is activated (Moreno Delgado et al., 2017; Kniazeff et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The sequence of the CRDs that link the VFTs to the HDs plays a role in coupling efficacy.
source: Of note, the sequence of the CRDs that link the VFTs to the HDs also plays a role, as indicated here by the differential coupling efficacies of receptor combinations containing either the mGlu2 CRD or the mGlu4 CRD (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4D.

claim: The second pathway of HD activation comes from a conformational change in the associated HD likely through a direct interaction between the two HDs in the dimer.
source: The second pathway comes from a conformational change in the associated HD likely through a direct interaction between the two HDs in the dimer, consistent with our previous data with the heterodimeric GABAB receptor (Monnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: The second component of HD activation is higher when the first, VFT mediated, is weak.
source: The second component is higher when the first, VFT mediated, is weak, due either to the activation of only one VFT (Figure 4), or to specific combinations of the CRDs (Figure 2, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, Figure 2, and Figure 4D.

claim: Allosteric interaction between HDs most likely results from a contact between the two HDs via an interface that can communicate information from one HD to the other.
source: Such allosteric interaction most likely results from a contact between the two HDs via an interface that can communicate information from one HD to the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both HDs in a class C GPCR contact each other through TM4 and 5 in the basal state.
source: Recently, we reported that, even though both HDs in a class C GPCR contact each other through TM4 and 5 in the basal state, as also reported for many class A GPCR dimers (Guo et al., 2005; Manglik et al., 2012), we surprisingly identified TM6 as being involved in the dimer interface of the active receptor dimer (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TM6 is involved in the dimer interface of the active receptor dimer.
source: Recently, we reported that, even though both HDs in a class C GPCR contact each other through TM4 and 5 in the basal state, as also reported for many class A GPCR dimers (Guo et al., 2005; Manglik et al., 2012), we surprisingly identified TM6 as being involved in the dimer interface of the active receptor dimer (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: TM6 is the TM that moves the most during class A GPCR activation.
source: TM6 is the TM that moves the most during class A GPCR activation (Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Rasmussen et al., 2011b), also likely in class C GPCRs (Pin and Bettler, 2016) for which the allosteric coupling between both HDs in a GPCR dimer is of fundamental mechanistic importance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible, using small molecules to reorient the G protein coupling from one subunit to the other – i.e. from the mGlu4 HD to the mGlu2 HD in the mGlu2-4 heterodimer.
source: Another major observation is that it is possible, using small molecules to reorient the G protein coupling from one subunit to the other – i.e. from the mGlu4 HD to the mGlu2 HD in the mGlu2-4 heterodimer (Figure 7, States 4a, 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: By either preventing the activation of the mGlu4 HD with an mGlu4 specific NAM, or by stabilizing the mGlu2 HD in its active conformation with a specific mGlu2 PAM, the G protein coupling is transferred from the mGlu4 to the mGlu2 subunit.
source: Indeed, by either preventing the activation of the mGlu4 HD with an mGlu4 specific NAM (Figure 7, States 4b), or by stabilizing the mGlu2 HD in its active conformation with a specific mGlu2 PAM (Figure 7, States 4b), the G protein coupling is transferred from the mGlu4 to the mGlu2 subunit.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The mGlu4 HD is likely more prone to reach a G protein activating state than the mGlu2 HD.
source: This observation suggests that the mGlu4 HD is likely more prone to reach a G protein activating state than the mGlu2 HD, and the fully active form of mGlu4 HD prevents the mGlu2 HD from reaching a G protein activating state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The fully active form of mGlu4 HD prevents the mGlu2 HD from reaching a G protein activating state.
source: This observation suggests that the mGlu4 HD is likely more prone to reach a G protein activating state than the mGlu2 HD, and the fully active form of mGlu4 HD prevents the mGlu2 HD from reaching a G protein activating state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Allosteric modulators are expected to have less side effects because they target a site that is under less pressure during evolution, such that it is possible to identify subtype selective molecules.
source: There is much interest in the development of allosteric modulators, since these are expected to have less side effects for several reasons (Changeux and Christopoulos, 2016; Conn et al., 2014; Foster and Conn, 2017; May et al., 2007). Such small molecules target a site that is under less pressure during evolution, such that it is possible to identify subtype selective molecules, in contrast to compound acting in the orthosteric binding site highly conserved between homologous receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: PAMs do not constantly activate the receptor, then do not favor receptor desensitization and internalization.
source: In addition, PAMs do not constantly activate the receptor, then do not favor receptor desensitization and internalization.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PAMs.

claim: PAMs enhance the action of endogenous ligands, they increase the response when and where needed for an improved physiological response.
source: Moreover, because they enhance the action of endogenous ligands, they increase the response when and where needed for an improved physiological response.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PAMs.

claim: Allosteric modulators have the ability to control the asymmetric activation of a GPCR dimer.
source: Here we reveal a novel property of such small molecules: their ability to control the asymmetric activation of a GPCR dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The present study illustrates the complex allosteric interaction occurring between two associated G protein-activating units, with both positive and negative interactions.
source: Taken together, the present study illustrates the complex allosteric interaction occurring between two associated G protein-activating units, with both positive and negative interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A conformational change in one subunit is needed for a full G protein activation by its associated subunit, although the interaction also prevents the first subunit from activating G proteins.
source: Indeed, a conformational change in one subunit is needed for a full G protein activation by its associated subunit, although the interaction also prevents the first subunit from activating G proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
